UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                            )                       Docket No. ER26-3515-000

                             MOTION TO INTERVENE AND
                       PROTEST OF TALEN ENERGY CORPORATION

        PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) and

Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability1 proposal should be rejected because it is

unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.               While Talen appreciates PJM’s goals of

protecting ratepayers from rising costs while maintaining reliability, the vehicle chosen by PJM to

arrive at that destination is a lemon and, as explained in the attached testimony of Zachary Ming

of Energy and Environmental Economics, Inc. (“E3”), will result in inaccurate price signals, early

and unnecessary generation resource retirements, and increased prices in the long-term. First and

foremost, however, PJM’s vehicle should not even be on the road because it does not comply with

well-established law.

        The IRAS Proposal fails to comply with PJM’s Operating Agreement and the Federal

Power Act (“FPA”).2 PJM claims that New Large Load is not similarly situated to other load,

including existing Large Load, and thus is not unduly discriminated against under the IRAS

Proposal. PJM’s argument is erroneous and conclusory. PJM cannot explain how New Large

Load is uniquely situated in the context of procuring new capacity and emergency curtailment. In

Requirement (“VRR”) Curve artificially limits competition in the existing capacity market. 8 The

result will initially be a capacity clearing price that fails to equal net Cost of New Entry (“CONE”),

I.        MOTION TO INTERVENE

          Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 14 Talen

respectfully submits this motion to intervene in the above-captioned proceeding. The formal legal

name of Talen is Talen Energy Corporation. Talen is a corporation organized and existing under

the laws of Delaware. Talen maintains its principal place of business at 2929 Allen Parkway, 22nd

Floor, Houston, Texas 77019. Talen is a leading independent power producer and energy

infrastructure company which owns and operates approximately 15.7 gigawatts of power

infrastructure in the United States. Talen produces and sells electricity, capacity, and ancillary

services into wholesale U.S. power markets, including and primarily in PJM. Accordingly, the

actions taken by the Commission in this matter will directly affect the interests of Talen. Talen

has a direct and material interest in the instant proceeding that no other party can adequately

represent. Talen therefore requests that the Commission grant this motion to intervene and permit

Talen to participate in this proceeding with full rights as a party thereto.

II.       PROTEST

          The existing RPM construct was designed to improve price stability, enhance reliability,

and produce accurate price signals to incentivize new generation build.15 The U.S. Supreme Court

observed that

                   [t]he capacity auction serves to identify the need for new generation:
                   A high clearing price in the capacity auction encourages new
                   generators to enter the market, increasing supply and thereby
                   lowering the clearing price in the same-day and next-day auctions

                 encourages retirement of existing high-cost generators.16

PJM has adapted its approach to capacity auctions over past decades to produce more accurate and

defined price signals. For example, PJM’s historical Capacity Credit Market (“CCM”) was

replaced by the reliability pricing model (“RPM”) twenty years ago because the CCM did “not

enable market participants to see the reliability problems in particular locations” and did “not

provide price signals that would elicit solutions to reliability problems in enough time before the

problem occurs. . . .”17 If the goal is to produce accurate price signals that send clear messages to

new generation to build or to existing and costly generation to retire, then the market—a simulated

competitive construct—cannot perform efficiently if PJM interferes with the capacity auctions by

implementing artificial caps on supply and demand. Yet, that is the imprudent design and purpose

of the IRAS Proposal.

         A.      PJM’s proposal to require New Large Loads to procure new capacity or be
                 subject to curtailment is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory, and
                 unlawfully encroaches on State jurisdiction.

         Section 205(b) of the FPA prohibits the Commission from approving unjust, unreasonable,

and unduly discriminatory tariffs.18 The regulated utility, as the movant under FPA Section 205,

carries the burden of proof that its proposal is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory

“[b]ecause a regulated utility is the party with access to the necessary information [and] bears the

risk of an undeveloped or inconclusive record.”19 “Discrimination is undue when there is a

           The Commission has explained that similarly situated does not mean that customers must

be without difference.21 Rather, “it means that there are no differences that are material to the

inquiry at hand.”22 The Commission has also held that “entities are similarly situated if they are

in the same position with respect to the ends that the law seeks to promote or the abuses that it

seeks to prevent, even if they are different in many other respects.” 23 For example, in Calpine

for purposes of providing reactive power because they were equally capable of providing that

service.25 In Iberdrola Renewables, Inc. v. Bonneville Power Admin.,26 the Commission held that

“non-[f]ederal resources are similarly situated to [f]ederal hydroelectric and thermal resources for

purposes of transmission curtailments because they all take firm transmission service.”27

                 1.       PJM’s requirement that only New Large Load execute contracts with
                          BYONC resources or be subject to curtailment is unjust, unreasonable, and

         PJM is only requiring New Large Load to contract with BYONC resources to avoid

curtailment. PJM does not dispute this disparate treatment. Instead, PJM attempts to argue that

New Large Load is not similarly situated to any other load. What PJM means is that the IRAS

to treat data centers differently given their “incomparably large energy demands, how quickly data

centers can come online, and their unique potential to impact the reliability of the electric grid”;28

and (2) an out-of-context statement by the Commission that “large loads constitute ‘a separate

category of load’ because of their “size, operational behavior, and unique potential to impact the

transmission system.”29 However, these are mere differences in customer profiles and cannot

support a finding of differences “that are material to the inquiry at hand.”30 The inquiry at hand is

         Nearly all new commercial load is capable of procuring new capacity. PJM does not limit

bilateral capacity markets to specific customers, nor does PJM limit capacity transactions to only

large loads. In fact, PJM’s Capacity Exchange system allows unit-specific bilateral transactions

of as little as 0.1 MW.31 This means that New Large Load, existing Large Load, new commercial

load, and others are “in the same position with respect to the ends that” the IRAS Proposal “seeks

to promote.”32

         Resources beyond just New Large Load are also capable of electing to curtail service

during emergency events, e.g., large commercial industrial customers and existing Large Load.

Existing Large Load is completely indistinguishable from New Large Load in this context, just as

new and existing generation resources were equally capable of providing reactive power service

in Calpine.33 This is also similar to federal and non-federal generation resources being equally

able to curtail transmission service in Iberdrola.34 Although the customers at issue in Iberdrola

were all taking firm transmission service, the only reason New Large Load would be taking a

different service here, i.e., IRAS, is because PJM would force them to do so.

MW quantity to be curtailed or which Electric Distributors will be instructed to curtail. The ability

to curtail load and the potential to receive IRAS payments for such action certainly and

is capable of being translated in written form to make such determinations and include those

Therefore, under FERC’s “rule of reason” doctrine, PJM must include specific language regarding

how it will determine the MW quantity to be curtailed and which Electric Distributors it will

instruct to do so. The potential for arbitrary and capricious decision-making in PJM’s process is

too great to move forward without such specification. Load being served under IRAS cannot make

informed commercial decisions if it must read tea leaves to determine when and how much it will

be curtailed in a region-wide reliability event.

         PJM carries the burden to prove that the IRAS Proposal is just and reasonable.42 The

unnecessary generation retirements, increased prices in the long term, and its implementation will

be left to an opaque process known only to PJM. The Commission cannot find such results to be

just and reasonable and thus must reject the IRAS Proposal.

                            c.       The IRAS proposal fails to account for New Large Load that
                                    previously contracted for capacity from existing resources.

         Chairman Laura Swett assured stakeholders that the Commission’s actions with respect to

large load reforms and procedures “are not intended to disrupt existing commercial agreements.”43

Talen has previously explained that PJM’s reliability backstop procurement (“RBP”) proposal

would result in such load paying incremental capacity charges under the RBP.44 This is harmful

to the entire market because “uncertainties regarding rate stability and contract sanctity can have

a chilling effect on investments and a seller’s willingness to enter into long-term contracts and this,

in turn, can harm customers in the long run.”45 PJM is inserting additional uncertainty into the

market through the forced interruption of service to certain New Large Loads that are not allocated

RBP capacity and costs. Accordingly, the IRAS Proposal fails to even treat New Large Load on

a consistent basis and unjustly introduces a chilling effect on investments in PJM.

States retain their exclusive jurisdiction to regulate retail transactions.46 The FPA follows the

Tenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which provides that “[t]he powers not delegated to

the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States

         The U.S. Supreme Court has clarified the “anti-commandeering doctrine” over years of

precedent. Most pertinent here, in New York v. United States,48 the Court held that “Congress may

not commandeer the States’ legislative processes by directly compelling them to enact and enforce

as a result of the State’s failure to take prompt possession. The option to establish waste sites was

encouraged through monetary incentives. The Court held that this choice “would effectively

‘commandeer’ States into the service of federal regulatory purposes” and in reality “the States’

‘choice’ is no choice at all.”50

         B.           Even if the IRAS Proposal stood on solid legal ground—which it does not—
                      the proposal is unjust and unreasonable because it will ultimately result in
                      increased costs and could lead to further unduly discriminatory behavior.

         It is a well-accepted economic principle that competitive markets result in fair prices for

goods, incentivize innovation, and encourage overall market efficiency, as further described in the

attached Affidavit of Zachary Ming.61 Such markets, however, are difficult to develop organically

in industries with high cost of entry. Governmental or quasi-governmental organizations may
